newsitem.title: FRANCE: Air France managers to meet this week.
newsitem.headline: Air France managers to meet this week.

text.p: Senior managers of the Air France airline and its Air France Europe subsidiary will meet later this week to learn details of the group's new productivity targets and merger plans, an airline executive said on Tuesday.
Some 100 Air France Europe managers and up to 200 from Air France are to attend the meeting, said the executive who declined to be named.

The executives are due to meet on Friday and Saturday, at Louveciennes, outside Paris, when the group's Pact for Competitive Growth will be unveiled, prior to being announced to all employees in September.

The pact is group chairman Christian Blanc's follow-up to a three-year productivity plan which expires this year and which was designed to bring the flagcarrier up to the competitiveness of its European rivals.

The timetable and details of a planned merger of the international carrier Air France with its domestic and regional unit Air France Europe will also be revealed. The merger was set for the beginning of 1997, following the failure to create a separate European subsidiary.
That merger plan meant there was no longer a job for Air France Europe's managing director, Jean-Pierre Courcol, who resigned on Monday.

"There has been no difference of opinion between Jean-Pierre Courcol and Christian Blanc. Jean-Pierre Courcol's mission was not about the merger but the creation of the European company," a company spokesman said. Courcol was hired last year to oversee the setting up of the European unit.

Attempts to create a European company out of Air France Europe broke down when its pilots refused to sign new contracts which would have meant taking pay cuts to bring them into line with their Air France counterparts. The merger means they will be forced into accepting the conditions of Air France pilots.
The two-day seminar will include a review of the current productivity plan, which aimed to boost Air France competitiveness by 30 percent and put the airline on track for break even in 1997.
The productivity plan, which included pay freezes and job cuts of 6,000 over the three years, was a condition for Air France receiving a 20 billion franc ($4 billion) state cash injection.

The international airline made a slender operating profit of 413 million francs for the 1995/96 year, its first operating profit since 1989, compared to a year-ago loss of 902 million. ($ = 5.048 French Francs)
